finding: The live range of $380-$1,475 is about right against the outside estimates, but we could not confirm it from first principles. No public source stating a labor time was found for the 2015 Corolla 1.8L or the 2016 Camry 2.5L, so only two classes have a full total. Implied totals at $120-$160 per hour: truck (2016 F-150 5.0L) about $171-$358; luxury (2015 BMW 328i N20) about $569-$944. Economy and midsize cannot be totalled; their pump alone costs $59-$138 (Corolla) and $74-$167 (Camry). The truck figure is well under every benchmark, and under the live floor of $380. Two things explain most of that gap: it prices the pump alone at online prices ($51-$198, against RepairPal's $525-$598 for parts, which shops mark up and which usually includes coolant and often a thermostat), and its one-hour labor figure is a parts seller's approximate time for the earlier 2011-2014 truck, where the outside estimates assume two to four hours for a belt-driven pump. So this is not evidence that the live floor is too high. The luxury total sits inside the live range. All four example engines have an external or electric pump; none is driven by the timing belt or chain, so nothing here tests the top of the range. The outside estimates say timing-belt-driven pumps take roughly 4-8 hours, which is what the $1,475 ceiling would have to cover.
extras: A quote often adds coolant and a cooling system bleed or pressure test, a thermostat, a drive belt, new pump bolts or gaskets, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies, coolant disposal, and sales tax. On engines where the timing belt drives the pump, shops normally quote the timing belt, tensioner and idlers in the same job, which raises the total a lot. The parts figures here are the pump (with its gasket where included) only.
